Hello everyone,

If you've ever built software for the EV (Electric Vehicle) charging industry, you know that the Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) is the undisputed standard for communication between Charge Points and Central Systems (CSMS).
But building a scalable, reliable, and secure OCPP-compliant system is notoriously difficult. Developers often struggle with guessing payload shapes, manually validating JSON schemas, implementing complex WebSocket framing, and handling connection drops.
That’s why I built ocpp-ws-io—a type-safe, production-ready OCPP WebSocket RPC client and server ecosystem for Node.js, built from the ground up with TypeScript.
Building a CSMS or a charge point simulator shouldn't require hand-writing validation logic or risking runtime errors from malformed payloads. ocpp-ws-io sol…

If you've ever spent time manually cleaning up Python imports after a review comment saying "wrong order" or "import the module, not the symbol", you'll appreciate this.
Important is a free, open-source VS Code extension that validates and auto-fixes Python import statements according to the Google Python Style Guide and PEP 8. It gives you real-time feedback as you type and can fix every issue it raises with a single command.

articles.author: Bhavin Sheth
articles.description:
While building AllInOneTools, I expected users to behave in a simple way:
User lands → uses search → finds tool → completes task.
But watching real usage showed something different.
Most users don’t start with search.
They start with scanning.
They scroll a little…
Not because search is bad.
But because visual recognition is faster than thinking.
When users arrive on a tools website, they usually come with a task like:
• Compress an image
But instead of typing the tool name immediately, many users try to spot it visually first.
If they see something like:
Image Tools
They instinctively move toward it.
This happens within seconds.
If users scan first, the homepage structure becomes extremely important.
Clear categories
All help users locate their task quickly.
Without this, users hesitate.
And hesitation often means they leave.
On AllInOneTools, I started showing tools directly inside categories instead of only showing category names.
That small change helped users confirm instantly:
“Yes, my tool is here.”
Confidence increased.
Clicks increased.
When users visit your website, do they:
• Use search first?
Would love to hear how others observe user behavior.
articles.title: Most users don’t search for a tool — they scan the page first

You can change your password. You can get a new credit card number. You can move to a new city. You cannot change your face. When facial recognition flags you incorrectly, there is no correction mechanism. When your biometric data is breached, the damage is permanent. Welcome to the age of biometric surveillance — a technology that has been deployed faster than any legal or ethical framework designed to govern it, on populations that never consented to it, with error rates that fall hardest on the people who were already most vulnerable to state and corporate power.

articles.author: Henry Han
articles.description:
Hello world!
My name is Henry Han, and my Korean name is Sehun Han. I lived in Nicaragua for 15 years and attended an American school, which made me fluent in English, Spanish, and Korean.
I love to work out, eat, go for drives, walk in parks, and enjoy anything related to keyboards.
I am a Computer Science graduate from Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) in South Korea. I was not very motivated at the time and got distracted by a lot of things. I have always regretted not trying my best during university; that feeling haunted me like a ghost. Even when I was working in other roles, such as Global Sales for a pharmaceutical company, I wasn't happy. I knew I had taken the role not because I was passionate about medicine, but because it was an easy way to avoid being jobless.
About a month ago, I left my job to dedicate my time to studying programming, computer science, and everything dev-related. I know it will be a rough market to get a job, especially with AI replacing many junior positions. However, I decided that I didn't want to run away anymore from the dreams of my younger self: to be a genius programmer, just like the hackers in Hollywood movies.
My plan is to study full-time for the next 1 to 2 years to land a junior developer role. My interests are in Backend development, and I created this blog for "Today I Learned" (TIL) posts and occasional journaling.
I am open to all networking and am looking forward to learning from the community. Hopefully, I can become highly skilled in this field and return the generosity.
Looking forward to start this journey, and also making friends along the way! 😊
P.S.: I do not want to put too much time in styling my posts (initially), so please excuse the messy formatting!
P.P.S: I am not a fan of AI generated articles, as they don't feel genuine to me. Most of my posts will be raw, unorganized piles of thoughts that I will try to make sense of, make them readable, and enjoyable.
articles.title: Beginning of My Journey
